Q1.answer: Whether normalizing each input window of a forecaster with its own recent (rolling-window) statistics reduces forecast error when the series level shifts after training, without harming accuracy when there is no shift.

Q2.answer: Level shifts are described as the most common failure mode of deployed forecasters, and because forecasters are normalized with fixed training statistics, a post-deployment level shift mis-scales every input and inflates error.
Q2.missing: The claim that level shift is the 'most common' failure mode is asserted, not evidenced (reference omitted).

Q3.answer: In prior evaluations the authors examined, normalization scheme and model size (capacity) were varied together [R3], confounding the two, so the effect of per-window normalization alone under level shift had not been isolated.
Q3.missing: Which specific prior works confound the two is unclear because references are omitted.

Q4.answer: They generated SynthLoad (a synthetic hourly series following [R4]), injected level shifts of s∈{0.2,0.4,0.6,0.8} training std, and compared a baseline (fixed training statistics), RWN (statistics of most recent 48 steps), and RWN-fixed (statistics frozen after first 48 post-shift steps), all using the same MLP across 5 seeds.

Q5.answer: They fixed model capacity (same MLP) so the comparison is capacity-controlled, isolating the effect of the normalization scheme from model size; the RWN-fixed ablation isolates how much of any gain requires continued adaptation of statistics versus a one-time re-estimation.
Q5.missing: Rationale for the specific 48-step window is not given (acknowledged as untuned).

Q6.answer: MAE was measured on SynthLoad with no shift and at shifts s=0.2,0.4,0.6,0.8, comparing baseline vs RWN, plus an RWN-fixed ablation, each over 5 random seeds (means ± std reported).
Q6.missing: Only aggregate numbers for the no-shift case are given in text; per-shift numeric values are only in Figure 1.

Q7.answer: With no shift, RWN and baseline were indistinguishable (0.409±0.007 vs 0.412±0.006). Under shift, RWN reduced MAE by 11–29% for s=0.2–0.6. Freezing statistics (RWN-fixed) recovered about two thirds of the gain, implying roughly one third of the gain comes from continued adaptation.
Q7.missing: Exact per-shift MAE values are not tabulated in text; only a range and a figure.

Q8.answer: In this controlled synthetic setting, per-window (rolling) normalization reduces error under moderate level shift without costing unshifted accuracy, and most of the benefit comes from re-estimating statistics once rather than from continuous adaptation.
Q8.missing: Establishment is limited to one synthetic series and one fixed model.

Q9.answer: It does not establish benefit at the largest shift (s=0.8, no clear benefit), does not establish results on real data, does not test other shift types, does not vary model capacity beyond a single fixed MLP, and does not test tuned windows or other architectures.
Q9.missing: The reason RWN fails at s=0.8 is not analyzed.

Q10.answer: A capacity-controlled comparison showing RWN removes moderate-shift error without harming unshifted accuracy, establishing a boundary at the largest shift, plus an ablation attributing about a third of the gain to continued adaptation.

Q11.answer: Synthetic data only, fixed model capacity, untuned normalization window, and only level shifts considered (no other distribution-shift types).

Q12.answer: Rolling-window normalization fixes error from moderate level shifts (11–29% MAE reduction for s≤0.6) at no cost to unshifted accuracy, but not for large shifts (s=0.8); and most of the gain comes from a one-time re-estimation of statistics rather than continuous adaptation.

objective_discrepancies: Objective asks 'where the finding stops', but the abstract's 'removes that error' overstates the bounded result (moderate shifts only, s=0.8 null), partially obscuring the stopping point.

The objective's 'how much of any gain depends on continuing to adapt' is answered, but split across an inconsistent 1/3 (contribution) vs 2/3-recovered (results) framing that a careful reader must reconcile.

Audience is non-forecasting researchers who lack knowledge of normalization practice and the benchmark, yet the paper never explains standard training-statistic normalization or SynthLoad's benchmark lineage inline.
